name: Hemp
subtitle: Cannabis sativa, industrial
description: Needs roughly a quarter of cotton's water, no pesticide, and returns nutrients to the soil it grows in. Yields two to three times more fibre per hectare than cotton, and softens with every wash rather than wearing out.
pros: Very low water use compared to cotton
Builds and enriches soil as it grows
Softens with wear instead of degrading
cons: Degumming and processing take real infrastructure
Cultivation is licence-restricted in some countries
Supply chains are small and mostly niche
availability: Niche. Hemp cultivation is licence-controlled in several South Asian countries, so retail supply is thin and mostly sold by small specialist labels.

name: Linen
subtitle: Flax
description: Rain-fed, almost no spray, and the entire plant is used with nothing wasted. Wears for decades and biodegrades completely. Creasing is the only real cost, and that is a matter of taste.
cons: Creases easily
Regional flax cultivation is limited, so yarn is often imported
availability: Widely sold as finished fabric, though flax itself is grown in relatively few regions and yarn is frequently imported and then woven locally.

name: Ramie
subtitle: China grass
description: Linen's profile with even greater strength and natural resistance to bacteria. The catch is degumming: turning stalk into yarn takes real chemistry and labour, which is why it stays niche.
pros: Similar low-impact growing profile to linen
cons: Degumming process is chemistry- and labour-intensive
Rarely available as a pure, unblended fabric
availability: Niche. Grown in limited regions and rarely reaches retail in pure form — usually blended into handloom cloth.

name: Handspun & Handwoven Cotton
subtitle: Hand-spun, hand-woven cotton (khadi-style)
description: The same cotton fibre, spun and woven by hand rather than by mill. That removes the mill electricity, the boiler, and most of the processing water. It also tends to breathe better than mill-woven cotton in hot climates.
pros: No mill electricity or boiler use
Far less processing water than mill cotton
cons: Slower to produce than mill cotton
Supply depends on local handloom traditions
availability: Found through handloom cooperatives, artisan markets and specialist weavers where hand-spinning traditions are active.

name: Recycled Cotton
subtitle: Post-industrial / post-consumer
description: Skips farming entirely, which is where nearly all of cotton's damage sits. Fibres come out shorter, so it is usually blended with virgin fibre to hold together.
pros: No new farming, water or pesticide footprint
cons: Shortened fibres usually need blending with virgin fibre
Blending can reduce durability slightly
availability: Growing category, mostly through brands using certified recycled content (look for a Global Recycled Standard claim).

name: Recycled Wool
subtitle: Shoddy yarn
description: Old woollens shredded and re-spun. No new grazing, no new methane, no scouring of raw fleece. This has been done at scale for decades in South Asian textile recycling clusters.
pros: No new grazing or methane footprint
cons: Shorter, weaker fibres than virgin wool
Usually blended for strength
availability: Used in blankets, shawls and increasingly in outerwear labels using recycled shoddy yarn.

name: Jute
subtitle: The golden fibre
description: Grows on rain alone almost anywhere, absorbs carbon fast while growing, and rots down to nothing. Too coarse for most clothing, so it mostly lives in bags and outerwear panels.
cons: Too coarse for most apparel
Limited to bags, accessories and some outerwear
availability: Widely and cheaply available, especially in bag, accessory and home-textile form; apparel-grade jute blends are a growing niche.

name: Lyocell
subtitle: TENCEL and similar closed-loop wood pulp fibres
description: Wood pulp dissolved in a solvent recovered at about 99% and reused. Soft, drapes beautifully, biodegrades. It is a regenerated fibre rather than a natural one, and its footprint is only as good as the forest it's sourced from.
pros: Solvent is recovered and reused at ~99%
cons: Footprint depends entirely on responsible forestry sourcing
Regenerated, not a raw natural fibre
availability: Growing fast in shirting and innerwear; look for a named brand process (e.g. TENCEL) rather than a generic 'lyocell' claim.

name: Organic Cotton
subtitle: GOTS certified
description: No synthetic pesticide or fertiliser, healthier soil, and a safer crop for the farming family. Still thirsty, and lower yields mean more land per shirt. Rain-fed organic cotton scores near 8; irrigated organic cotton scores closer to 6.
cons: Still a water-intensive crop
Lower yields than conventional cotton, needing more land
availability: Available through certified organic cotton supply chains; look for a GOTS certificate to confirm the claim.

name: Alpaca
subtitle: South American camelid
description: A low-impact grazing animal, with wool that is warm, soft and durable. Regional supply outside South America is limited.
cons: Very limited regional supply outside South America
Higher cost
availability: Rare outside South America; mostly imported where sold at all.

name: Wool
subtitle: Extensive or regenerative grazing
description: Methane and land use are real costs. Against them: decades of wear, rarely needs washing, insulates even when wet, and biodegrades. Impact per wear is genuinely low. Intensive factory-farmed systems drop this score to around 5.
pros: Decades of wear from a single garment
cons: Methane emissions from grazing animals
Land-use footprint
Intensive farming systems score notably worse
availability: Widely available; apparel-grade wool (as opposed to carpet-grade) is often imported merino.

name: Eri Silk
subtitle: Ahimsa / peace silk
description: The moth leaves the cocoon before the silk is taken, so nothing is boiled alive. Reared on castor leaves with minimal input. Warmer and more matte than mulberry silk.
pros: Moth is not killed in production ('peace silk')
Warmer, more matte texture than mulberry silk
cons: Niche, regionally concentrated production
Higher price point
availability: Produced in specific regions with an established ahimsa silk tradition; sold through specialist and handloom outlets.

name: Pashmina
subtitle: Changthangi goat wool
description: Tiny volumes, hand-combed, and a genuine shawl outlives its owner. The risk is the high-altitude grassland the goats graze on, which is fragile and under grazing pressure.
cons: High-altitude grassland under grazing pressure
Extremely low volumes
Frequently faked or diluted with synthetic fibre
availability: Rare and expensive; only genuine, certified (GI-tagged where applicable) pashmina reflects the real fibre — cheap 'pashmina' is almost always viscose or acrylic.

name: Mulberry Silk
subtitle: Bombyx mori
description: Tiny land use and fully biodegradable, but reeling is water- and energy-heavy, and the pupae are killed in the cocoon. A silk garment is also often kept for generations, which counts for a great deal.
pros: Often kept and passed down for generations
cons: Water- and energy-heavy reeling process
Pupae are killed during production
availability: Widely available; look for a silk-authentication mark to rule out polyester sold as silk.

name: Modal
subtitle: Certified beech pulp
description: A softer cousin of viscose, made with recovered chemicals when it comes from a reputable, certified producer. Uncertified modal is essentially just viscose with a nicer name.
pros: Certified producers recover and reuse processing chemicals
cons: Uncertified modal offers no real advantage over standard viscose
Regenerated fibre, chemically intensive process
availability: Common in innerwear and loungewear; a named certified process (e.g. Lenzing Modal) is worth paying more for.

name: Conventional Cotton
subtitle: BT / hybrid
description: Around 2,700 litres of water for one t-shirt. Cotton covers about 2.5% of the world's farmland but takes a far larger share of its insecticide use. It does at least biodegrade, and it remains one of the most widely worn fibres.
pros: Extremely widely available at every price point
cons: Very high water use (~2,700 litres per t-shirt)
Disproportionately high pesticide/insecticide use
availability: Available everywhere, at every price point — the most common fibre in the market.

name: Leather (Vegetable-Tanned)
subtitle: Bark tanned
description: Carries the full cattle footprint, which is heavy. Against it: bark tanning avoids chromium effluent, and good shoes made this way can last fifteen to twenty years — far longer than most alternatives.
pros: Can last 15-20 years when well made
cons: Full cattle production footprint
Harder to find; smaller-scale tanneries
availability: Made by small, specialist tanneries — usually needs to be specifically requested by name.
recommendedUses: Bags and belts kept for years

name: Recycled Polyester
subtitle: rPET from bottles
description: The best of the plastics. It skips virgin fossil feedstock and diverts bottles from waste, and for a rain jacket or running shirt it is the right call. But it sheds microfibre exactly like virgin polyester, and bottle-to-fabric is a one-way trip, not a closed loop.
pros: Diverts plastic bottles from waste streams
cons: Sheds microfibre exactly like virgin polyester
Not itself recyclable again ('one-way trip')
availability: Common in activewear; look for a Global Recycled Standard (GRS) certificate rather than a bare claim.

name: Viscose / Rayon
subtitle: Conventional, Liva-type
description: Dissolved wood pulp made using carbon disulfide, a solvent dangerous to mill workers and often released untreated. Linked to logging of ancient and endangered forest.
cons: Carbon disulfide is dangerous to mill workers
Often released untreated into the environment
Linked to logging of ancient/endangered forest
availability: Extremely common in inexpensive printed fabrics, dresses and everyday clothing.
recommendedUses: Printed dresses and everyday wear (best avoided where alternatives exist)

name: Bamboo Fabric
subtitle: = bamboo viscose
description: Bamboo the plant is excellent. Bamboo the fabric sold in stores is almost always viscose: the stalk is dissolved using the same harsh chemistry as conventional viscose, and none of the plant's environmental virtue survives that process.
pros: The raw plant itself grows quickly with little input
cons: Marketed as 'natural' but is chemically processed viscose
Same carbon disulfide process as conventional viscose
None of bamboo's growing benefits carry through
availability: Sold widely as an 'eco' product — treat any bamboo fabric label as viscose, not as raw bamboo.
recommendedUses: Best treated the same as conventional viscose

name: Cashmere
subtitle: Changra / Mongolian goat
description: Each goat gives only a few hundred grams a year, so rising demand has multiplied herd sizes. Goats pull grass out by the root, and overgrazing has driven serious desertification in cashmere-producing grasslands.
cons: Overgrazing has driven serious grassland desertification
Low yield per animal drives large herd sizes
Most retail cashmere is imported and frequently diluted or fake
availability: Genuine cashmere is a premium product; much of what's sold cheaply is not real cashmere.
recommendedUses: Occasional fine knitwear, bought to last

name: Leather (Chrome-Tanned)
subtitle: Standard commercial
description: The cattle footprint plus a tanning process using chromium salts. Where effluent treatment is weak, that chromium reaches groundwater. About 85% of the world's leather is tanned this way.
cons: Chromium effluent risk where treatment is weak
Full cattle production footprint
availability: The default in commercial footwear and bags — the vast majority of leather goods sold.
recommendedUses: Everyday footwear and bags (veg-tanned is the lower-impact alternative)

name: Polyester
subtitle: Virgin PET
description: Made from crude oil and gas, and now more than half of all fibre produced on Earth. Sheds plastic in every wash, and a discarded polyester shirt outlives the person who bought it by centuries.
cons: Made from fossil feedstock
Sheds microplastic in every wash
Effectively never biodegrades
availability: The default, most affordable fabric across the clothing market.
recommendedUses: Budget-conscious basics (best chosen in recycled form where possible)

name: Nylon / Polyamide
subtitle: PA6, PA66
description: Everything polyester does, plus a production route that releases nitrous oxide, a greenhouse gas roughly 273 times more warming than carbon dioxide. Extremely strong, which is its only real defence.
cons: Production releases nitrous oxide (~273x the warming potency of CO2)
Fossil-based, sheds microplastic, does not biodegrade
availability: Common in linings, sportswear, swimwear and umbrellas.
recommendedUses: Where genuine strength/stretch is required (swimwear, sportswear)

name: Poly-Cotton Blend
subtitle: PC 65/35 and similar
description: The worst of both parents: cotton's water and pesticide load, polyester's fossil feedstock and shedding, and a mix that no recycler can separate.
cons: Combines the footprints of both fibres
Cannot be separated for recycling at end of life
availability: Extremely common in uniforms, office shirts and bedsheets — among the most-worn fabrics globally.
recommendedUses: Avoid where a single-fibre alternative exists

name: Acrylic
subtitle: Polyacrylonitrile (PAN)
description: The heaviest microfibre shedder measured in a domestic wash, releasing several times more than polyester in the same load. Pills badly and is thrown away quickly as a result.
cons: Heaviest microfibre shedder of any common fabric
Pills quickly, short usable life
availability: Common in inexpensive sweaters, mufflers and 'woollen' winterwear.
recommendedUses: Best avoided where a wool or recycled-wool alternative is affordable

name: Elastane / Spandex
subtitle: Lycra, spandex
description: Some clothes genuinely need it — socks, underwear, swimwear and activewear do not work well without stretch, and there is no realistic way around that. The problem is elastane in garments that never needed it: shirts, denim, bedsheets. Even a 2% share means the garment cannot be recycled.
cons: Even a small percentage makes a garment unrecyclable
Frequently added to garments that don't need stretch
availability: Common as a small percentage in shirting and denim, and essential in socks and activewear.

name: PVC 'Vegan Leather'
subtitle: Polyvinyl chloride
description: The floor of this scorecard. Softened with phthalates, releases dioxins when made or burned, and cracks and fails within about two years. 'Vegan' here means plastic, not necessarily low-impact.
cons: Softened with phthalates
Releases dioxins in production or when burned
Typically fails within ~2 years
availability: Common in cheap bags, belts, jackets and shoes; PU is a marginally better plastic alternative.
recommendedUses: Best avoided — consider veg-tanned leather, canvas or recycled polyester instead
